geology.description: The study of the Earth—its history, structure, composition, life forms, and the processes that continue to change it.

formation.description: A body of rock that is sufficiently distinctive and continuous that it can be mapped.

stratigraphy.description: The study of the history, composition, relative ages and distribution of strata, and the interpretation of strata to elucidate Earth history.

lithology.description: The macroscopic nature of the mineral content, grain size, texture and color of rocks.

fault.description: A break or planar surface in brittle rock across which there is observable displacement.

basin.description: A depression in the crust of the Earth, caused by plate tectonic activity and subsidence, in which sediments accumulate.

geophysics.description: The study of the physics of the Earth, especially its electrical, gravitational, and magnetic fields and propagation of elastic (seismic) waves within it.

petrophysics.description: The study of physical and chemical rock properties and their interactions with fluids.

resistivity.description: The ability of a material to resist electrical conduction.

borehole geophysics.description: The acquisition and analysis of physical measurements made by instruments lowered into a wellbore.

gravity anomaly.description: The difference between the observed gravity and a value predicted from a model, indicating subsurface density variations.

sedimentology.description: The study of modern sediments such as sand, silt, and clay, and the processes that result in their formation, transport, deposition, and diagenesis.

depositional environment.description: The physical, chemical, and biological conditions under which a sediment accumulates.

facies.description: The overall characteristics of a rock unit that reflect its origin and differentiate the unit from others around it.

compaction.description: The physical process by which sediments are consolidated, resulting in the reduction of pore space as grains are packed closer together.

diagenesis.description: The physical, chemical or biological alteration of sediments into sedimentary rock at relatively low temperatures and pressures that can result in changes to the rock's original mineralogy and texture.

shale.description: A fine-grained, fissile, detrital sedimentary rock formed by consolidation of clay- and silt-sized particles into thin, relatively impermeable layers.

sandstone.description: A clastic sedimentary rock whose grains are predominantly sand-sized.

palynology.description: The study of fossilized remnants of microscopic entities having organic walls, such as pollen, spores and cysts from algae.

pollen.description: Fine dust-like grains produced by seed plants, used in palynology for biostratigraphy and paleoenvironmental reconstruction.

spore.description: An organic-walled reproductive structure produced by non-flowering plants, key in palynological geological dating.

palynomorph.description: A microscopic, organic-walled fossil structure studied in palynology.

biostratigraphy.description: The application of plant and animal fossils to date and correlate strata in order to elucidate Earth history, combining the principles of paleontology and stratigraphy.

paleontology.description: The study of fossilized, or preserved, remnants of plant and animal life.

fossil.description: Preserved remnants of plants or animals, such as skeletons, shells, casts or molds, tracks or borings, and feces.

index fossil.description: A fossil that is useful for dating and correlating the strata in which it is found (usually widespread, short-lived).

biozone.description: A stratigraphic interval defined by its fossil content.

paleoecology.description: The study of ancient ecosystems and the interactions between fossil organisms and their environments.

production.description: The phase that occurs after successful exploration and development and during which hydrocarbons are drained from an oil or gas field.

flow rate.description: The volume of fluid that passes through a given cross-section per unit time.

gas lift.description: An artificial lift method where compressed gas is injected into the production tubing to reduce hydrostatic pressure and aid fluid flow.

enhanced oil recovery.description: Techniques (thermal, gas injection, chemical) used to increase the amount of crude oil that can be extracted from a reservoir.

artificial lift.description: Any system used to bring fluids to the surface when a well does not flow naturally.

water cut.description: The ratio of water produced compared to the total volume of liquids produced.

well completion.description: The downhole tubulars, packers, safety valves, and surface equipment installed to prepare a drilled well for safe and efficient production.

packer.description: A device that can be run into a wellbore with a smaller initial outside diameter that then expands externally to seal the wellbore.

perforation.description: The communication tunnel created from the casing or liner into the reservoir formation, through which oil or gas is produced.

completion fluid.description: A solids-free liquid placed in the wellbore before completion operations to control well pressure.

christmas tree.description: An assembly of valves, spools, and fittings installed at the wellhead to control fluid flow from the well.

drilling.description: The operations involved in boring a hole into the Earth's crust to explore or extract resources.

drill string.description: The column of pipe, tool joints, and bottomhole assembly that transmits rotation and fluid to the drill bit.

mud motor.description: A hydraulic motor placed in the drill string that uses drilling fluid flow to rotate the drill bit.

bottom hole assembly.description: The lowest portion of the drill string, comprising the bit, stabilizers, collars, and measurement tools.

casing.description: Large-diameter pipe lowered into an openhole and cemented in place.

drilling fluid.description: Mud circulated down the drill string and up the annulus to cool the bit, transport cuttings, and control subsurface pressure.

well stimulation.description: Treatments performed to restore or enhance productivity, such as hydraulic fracturing or acidizing.

hydraulic fracturing.description: Injecting high-pressure fluid into a formation to create fractures and increase reservoir permeability.

proppant.description: Sized particles mixed with fracturing fluid to hold fractures open after a hydraulic fracturing treatment.

slickwater.description: A water-based fracturing fluid containing friction reducers to allow high-rate injection.

acidizing.description: The pumping of acid into the wellbore to remove near-well formation damage and other damaging substances.

seismic.description: Relating to earthquakes, vibrations, or subsurface elastic wave propagation used for modeling.

seismic section.description: A 2D cross-sectional plot of seismic reflection traces showing subsurface structural features.

acoustic impedance.description: The product of seismic velocity and density, critical for determining reflection coefficients.

reflector.description: An interface between layers of contrasting acoustic, optical or electromagnetic properties.

seismic acquisition.description: The generation and recording of seismic data using energy sources and wave detectors.

geophone.description: A device used in surface seismic acquisition, both onshore and on the seabed offshore, that detects ground velocity produced by seismic waves and transforms the motion into electrical impulses.

hydrophone.description: A device designed for use in detecting seismic energy in the form of pressure changes underwater during marine seismic acquisition.

vibroseis.description: A land seismic energy source that generates a controlled vibratory signal.

shotpoint.description: One of a number of locations or stations at the surface of the Earth at which a seismic source is activated.

air gun.description: A marine seismic energy source that releases high-pressure bubbles of air into the water.

outcrop.description: A body of rock exposed at the surface of the Earth.

fold.description: A wave-like geologic structure that forms when rocks deform by bending instead of breaking under compressional stress.

unconformity.description: A geological surface separating older from younger rocks and representing a gap in the geologic record.
